course.description: A comprehensive 40-part course designed to transform you into a confident competitive programmer. Covers STL deep-dive, all essential data structures, algorithms, number theory, combinatorics, graph theory, dynamic programming, string algorithms, and advanced CP techniques with real contest examples and code.

blocks.value: The Competitive Programming Mindset

Competitive Programming (CP) is not just about knowing algorithms — it's about solving problems under time pressure with optimal code. In CP, every millisecond and every byte of memory matters. Your goal is to write correct, efficient, and concise code that passes all test cases within strict limits.

blocks.alt: Timeline showing problem reading, analysis, coding, testing, and submission in a contest
blocks.caption: CP is a race against time — optimize your workflow from reading to submission

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Infographic — Horizontal timeline with 5 stages: 1) Read Problem (clock icon, 2-3 min), 2) Analyze & Design (brain icon, 5-10 min), 3) Code (keyboard icon, 10-20 min), 4) Test (bug icon, 5 min), 5) Submit (checkmark icon). Show time estimates. Use contest-themed colors (dark background, neon accents).
Why C++ Dominates CP

C++ is the #1 language in competitive programming for good reasons:
• **Speed** — Compiled to machine code, no VM overhead like Java/Python
• **STL** — Rich, optimized library of data structures and algorithms
• **Control** — Fine-grained memory and performance tuning
• **Templates** — Generic code that works with any type
• **Community** — Most tutorials, editorials, and solutions are in C++

Top platforms (Codeforces, AtCoder, LeetCode) show 70-80% of top submissions in C++.
The CP Template — Your Starting Point
Every CP coder has a template. It includes fast I/O, common macros, and type aliases. This saves precious seconds in contests. Here's a battle-tested template used by top coders.
Fast I/O — The #1 Optimization

By default, C++ iostream is synchronized with C stdio for compatibility. This makes it SLOW. `ios::sync_with_stdio(false)` disables this sync. `cin.tie(nullptr)` decouples cin from cout so cin doesn't flush cout before reading. Together, they make iostream as fast as scanf/printf.
Understanding Time & Memory Limits

**Time Complexity Guide:**
• n ≤ 10: O(n!), O(2^n) brute force OK
• n ≤ 20: O(2^n) with bitmasks
• n ≤ 100: O(n^3) dynamic programming
• n ≤ 1,000: O(n^2) algorithms
• n ≤ 10^5: O(n log n) sorting, binary search
• n ≤ 10^6: O(n) linear scan
• n ≤ 10^7: O(n) with tight constants
• n > 10^7: O(1) or O(log n) only

**Memory:** 1 int = 4 bytes. Array of 10^6 ints = 4 MB. Most contests allow 256-1024 MB.
Common CP Platforms

**Codeforces** — Most popular, 2-3 hour contests, Div 1-4 rated. Problems A-E (or F).
**AtCoder** — Japanese platform, Beginner/Regular contests, strong math focus.
**LeetCode** — Interview prep, weekly contests, topic-focused.
**CodeChef** — Indian platform, Long Challenges (10 days), Cook-Off, Lunchtime.
**HackerRank** — Structured learning, interview practice.
**TopCoder** — Classic platform, SRMs (Single Round Matches).

blocks.question: What is the maximum n for which O(n^2) algorithm is acceptable in 1 second?
blocks.explanation: O(n^2) with n=1000 is ~1 million operations, which runs in under 0.1s. For n=10^5, n^2 = 10^10 operations — way too slow (would take ~10+ seconds).

blocks.question: What does cin.tie(nullptr) do?
options: Decouples cin from cout so cin doesn't flush cout
blocks.correctAnswer: Decouples cin from cout so cin doesn't flush cout
blocks.explanation: By default, cin flushes cout before reading. tie(nullptr) removes this coupling, preventing unnecessary flushes and speeding up I/O significantly.

blocks.question: Which header includes all standard C++ libraries at once for CP?
blocks.explanation: #include <bits/stdc++.h> is a GCC feature that includes every standard library header. It's accepted on most CP platforms and saves typing time in contests.

blocks.value: vector: Your Go-To Container

`std::vector` is the most used container in CP. It's a dynamic array with O(1) random access, O(1) amortized push_back, and cache-friendly contiguous memory. Mastering vector operations is essential for solving array-based problems efficiently.

blocks.alt: Visual showing vector internal structure with capacity doubling when full
blocks.caption: Vectors double capacity when full — O(1) amortized push_back

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Top row: vector with 4 elements, capacity 4, all slots filled. Arrow labeled 'push_back(5)'. Bottom row: new vector with capacity 8 (doubled), 5 elements copied, new element 5 added. Show old memory freed. Label 'O(n) reallocation' but 'O(1) amortized per operation'.
Essential Vector Operations for CP

Know these operations by heart — you'll use them in almost every problem:
• `v.push_back(x)` — Add to end (amortized O(1))
• `v.pop_back()` — Remove last (O(1))
• `v.back()` — Access last element (O(1))
• `v.empty()` — Check if empty (O(1))
• `v.size()` — Number of elements (O(1))
• `v.clear()` — Remove all elements (O(n))
• `v.resize(n)` — Change size (O(n))
• `v.reserve(n)` — Pre-allocate capacity (O(n))

First: 10, Last: 30

blocks.value: 2D Vectors — The Grid Container
2D vectors are essential for grid problems, adjacency matrices, and DP tables. Initialize properly to avoid segmentation faults. Use `v.assign(rows, vector<int>(cols, 0))` for clean initialization.
CP Example: Running Maximum
Problem: Given an array, find the running maximum at each position. This is a classic warm-up that tests basic vector manipulation and loop skills.
CP Example: Two Pointer Technique
Problem: Find if there exists a pair in a sorted array that sums to target. The two-pointer technique is O(n) vs O(n^2) brute force. Sort first (O(n log n)), then use two pointers from both ends.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of vector::push_back()?
blocks.explanation: push_back is O(1) amortized. Occasionally it triggers O(n) reallocation when capacity is full, but over many operations the average is O(1). Use reserve() if you know the size upfront.

blocks.question: How do you create a 2D vector of size n×m initialized to 0?
blocks.explanation: vector<vector<int>> v(n, vector<int>(m, 0)) creates n rows, each with m columns initialized to 0. The inner vector<int>(m, 0) is copied n times.

blocks.question: Which vector method removes the last element in O(1) time?
blocks.explanation: pop_back() removes the last element in O(1) time. It does not return the removed element — use back() first if you need it.

blocks.value: Pair, Tuple & Custom Sorting

`std::pair` and `std::tuple` are lightweight containers for grouping related data. They're essential for returning multiple values, storing coordinates, edges in graphs, and key-value associations. Combined with custom sorting, they solve countless CP problems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing pair as two connected boxes and tuple as multiple connected boxes
blocks.caption: pair holds 2 elements; tuple holds any number of elements

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Top: pair<int, int> as two connected boxes labeled 'first' and 'second'. Bottom: tuple<int, string, double> as three connected boxes. Show make_pair() and make_tuple() constructors. Use clean, minimal style.
pair Essentials

`pair<T1, T2>` stores two values of possibly different types. Access with `.first` and `.second`. Use `make_pair()` or brace initialization. Pairs are comparable — they compare lexicographically (first, then second).
tuple for 3+ Values
Use `tuple` when you need more than 2 values. Access elements with `get<index>(t)`. C++17 introduced structured bindings for cleaner tuple/pair unpacking.
Custom Sorting with Lambda

`sort()` with a custom comparator is one of the most powerful CP techniques. Use lambda functions for inline, concise comparators. Sort by any criteria: descending, by second element, by absolute value, etc.
CP Example: Activity Selection (Greedy)
Problem: Given n activities with start and end times, select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities. The greedy strategy: sort by end time, then always pick the activity that ends earliest.

blocks.question: How do you access the second element of a pair<int, int> named p?
blocks.explanation: pair has two public members: first and second. Use p.first and p.second to access them. They are not accessed via index or get().

blocks.question: Which C++17 feature allows clean unpacking of tuples?
blocks.explanation: Structured bindings (C++17) allow auto [a, b, c] = tuple; syntax for clean unpacking. Before C++17, you had to use tie() or get<>().

blocks.question: Which function sorts a vector with a custom comparator in C++?
blocks.explanation: std::sort(begin, end, comparator) sorts the range. The comparator is a function/lambda returning true if a should come before b. Default is ascending order.

parts.partTitle: Part 4: STL Set, Multiset & Ordered Statistics

blocks.value: set, multiset & Order Statistics

`std::set` stores unique elements in sorted order with O(log n) insertion, deletion, and lookup. `std::multiset` allows duplicates. Both use Red-Black trees internally. For CP, they're essential for maintaining dynamic sorted data and order statistics.

blocks.alt: Red-Black tree visualization showing balanced binary search tree with set elements
blocks.caption: set uses a balanced BST — all operations are O(log n)

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A balanced binary search tree (Red-Black tree) with nodes 10, 5, 15, 3, 7, 12, 20. Show the tree is balanced (black height equal). Label operations: insert, delete, find all O(log n). Use tree visualization with color-coded nodes (red/black).
set Operations for CP

**insert(x)** — O(log n), returns pair<iterator, bool>
**erase(x)** — O(log n), removes element (or iterator)
**find(x)** — O(log n), returns iterator or end()
**count(x)** — O(log n), returns 0 or 1 (set), or multiplicity (multiset)
**lower_bound(x)** — O(log n), first element >= x
**upper_bound(x)** — O(log n), first element > x
**begin()/end()** — O(1), smallest/largest (with rbegin for reverse)

blocks.value: multiset for Duplicates

`multiset` allows duplicate values. `count()` returns the number of occurrences. `erase(x)` removes ALL occurrences — use `erase(iterator)` to remove just one. Be careful with `find()` — it returns an iterator to ONE occurrence.

blocks.value: Order Statistics Tree (Policy-Based DS)

GNU C++ provides **policy-based data structures** that extend set with two powerful operations: `find_by_order(k)` — returns iterator to k-th smallest element (0-indexed), and `order_of_key(x)` — returns number of elements strictly less than x. Both are O(log n). This is a game-changer for CP.
CP Example: Running Median

Problem: Given a stream of numbers, find the median after each insertion. Use two multisets: a max-heap (left half) and a min-heap (right half). Balance them so their sizes differ by at most 1. The median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of set::insert()?
blocks.explanation: set uses a balanced BST (Red-Black tree). Insertion requires traversing the tree height, which is O(log n) for n elements.

blocks.question: In a policy-based ordered_set, what does order_of_key(x) return?
options: The number of elements strictly less than x
The number of elements equal to x
blocks.correctAnswer: The number of elements strictly less than x
blocks.explanation: order_of_key(x) returns the count of elements strictly less than x, which is essentially the rank/position x would have if inserted.

blocks.question: Which multiset method returns an iterator to the first element not less than x?
blocks.explanation: lower_bound(x) returns an iterator to the first element >= x. upper_bound(x) returns the first element > x. Both are O(log n) in set/multiset.

parts.partTitle: Part 5: STL Map, Unordered_Map & Frequency Counting

blocks.value: map, unordered_map & Frequency Problems

`std::map` is an ordered key-value store with O(log n) operations. `std::unordered_map` uses hash tables for average O(1) operations. For CP, unordered_map is preferred for pure lookups, while map is needed when order matters or for lower_bound queries.

blocks.alt: Comparison showing map as sorted tree vs unordered_map as hash table with buckets
blocks.caption: map is ordered (BST); unordered_map is hashed (average O(1))

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Left: 'std::map' as a balanced BST with sorted keys. Right: 'std::unordered_map' as a hash table with buckets and chaining. Label time complexities: map O(log n) all ops, unordered_map O(1) average, O(n) worst. Use contrasting styles (tree vs buckets).
map vs unordered_map — When to Use

**Use map when:**
• You need elements in sorted order
• You need lower_bound/upper_bound
• Worst-case O(n) from hash collisions is unacceptable

**Use unordered_map when:**
• You only need fast lookups/inserts/deletes
• Order doesn't matter
• Keys have a good hash function

**CP Tip:** unordered_map can be hacked with collision attacks on some platforms. Use `reserve()` and `max_load_factor()` to mitigate, or use gp_hash_table from ext/pb_ds.

blocks.value: CP Example: Two Sum (Hash Map)

Problem: Find two numbers in an array that add up to target. The hash map solution is O(n) — iterate once, storing each number's complement (target - num) in the map. This is a classic CP interview problem.
CP Example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

Problem: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Use a sliding window with a hash map tracking the last seen index of each character. When a repeat is found, shrink the window from the left.
CP Example: Count Distinct Elements in Subarrays

Problem: Given an array and queries [L,R], count distinct elements in each range. Use Mo's Algorithm (sqrt decomposition) or a Fenwick tree with last occurrence tracking. Here's the last-occurrence approach for offline queries.

blocks.question: What is the average time complexity of unordered_map operations?
blocks.explanation: unordered_map uses hash tables, giving average O(1) for insert, delete, and find. Worst case is O(n) due to collisions, but this is rare with a good hash function.

blocks.question: Which map method returns the number of elements with a given key?
blocks.explanation: map::count(key) returns 1 if the key exists, 0 otherwise. For multiset, it returns the number of occurrences. find() returns an iterator, not a count.

blocks.question: Which C++11 loop syntax iterates over key-value pairs in a map?
blocks.explanation: for (auto& [key, value] : map) is the C++17 structured binding syntax. In C++11, use for (auto& pair : map) and access pair.first/pair.second.

blocks.value: Stack, Queue & Deque — Linear Containers

These three containers represent fundamental abstract data types. **Stack** is LIFO (Last In, First Out). **Queue** is FIFO (First In, First Out). **Deque** (Double-Ended Queue) allows insertion and deletion at both ends. All three are essential for CP — from bracket matching to BFS to sliding window problems.

blocks.alt: Visual comparison of Stack (LIFO), Queue (FIFO), and Deque (both ends)
blocks.caption: Stack: push/pop at one end. Queue: enqueue at back, dequeue from front. Deque: both ends.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Three vertical sections. Left: Stack as a vertical tube with items pushed/popped from top only. Label 'LIFO'. Middle: Queue as a horizontal conveyor belt, items enter at back, exit from front. Label 'FIFO'. Right: Deque as a horizontal tube open at both ends. Label 'Both ends'. Use distinct colors per container.
stack — LIFO Container

`stack<T>` provides: `push(x)` — add to top, `pop()` — remove top, `top()` — access top, `empty()` — check if empty, `size()` — element count. All operations are O(1). The underlying container is deque by default.
queue — FIFO Container
`queue<T>` provides: `push(x)` — add to back, `pop()` — remove front, `front()` — access front, `back()` — access back, `empty()`, `size()`. All O(1). Essential for BFS and task scheduling problems.
deque — Double-Ended Queue

`deque<T>` combines stack and queue: `push_back()`, `push_front()`, `pop_back()`, `pop_front()`, `front()`, `back()`, `[]` random access. All O(1). It's the underlying container for stack and queue, but exposed directly it's incredibly powerful for sliding window problems.
CP Example: Valid Parentheses (Stack)

Problem: Given a string of brackets, determine if it's valid (every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in correct order). This is the classic stack interview problem and a Codeforces Div 2 A staple.

blocks.value: CP Example: Sliding Window Maximum (Deque)

Problem: Given an array and window size k, find the maximum in every contiguous subarray of size k. The deque solution is O(n) — maintain a deque of indices where elements are in decreasing order. Remove elements outside the window and smaller than current.

blocks.question: Which container follows LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle?
blocks.explanation: stack is LIFO — the last element pushed is the first one popped. queue is FIFO, deque allows both ends, and priority_queue orders by priority.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of deque::push_front()?
blocks.explanation: All deque operations (push_front, push_back, pop_front, pop_back, front, back) are O(1). Deque uses a chunked array structure that allows efficient operations at both ends.

blocks.question: Which deque method removes an element from the front?
blocks.explanation: pop_front() removes the first element from the deque in O(1) time. It's one of the key advantages of deque over vector for front-removal operations.

blocks.value: Priority Queue — The Heap Container

`std::priority_queue` is a max-heap by default — the largest element is always at the top. It provides O(1) access to the maximum, O(log n) insertion and deletion. For CP, it's essential for greedy algorithms, Dijkstra's algorithm, merging k sorted arrays, and median maintenance.

blocks.alt: Max-heap tree visualization with 50 at root and smaller elements below
blocks.caption: Max-heap: parent is always >= children. Top() returns the maximum in O(1).

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A complete binary tree (max-heap) with 50 at root, children 30 and 20, etc. Show that every parent >= children. Label operations: top() O(1), push/pop O(log n). Use tree visualization with heap property highlighted.
priority_queue Basics

**push(x)** — O(log n), insert element
**pop()** — O(log n), remove top
**top()** — O(1), access maximum (or minimum for min-heap)
**empty()**, **size()** — O(1)

Default is max-heap. For min-heap, use `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>`.

blocks.value: CP Example: K Largest Elements

Problem: Find the k largest elements in an array. Use a min-heap of size k — iterate through the array, if the heap has fewer than k elements, push current. Otherwise, if current > heap top, pop top and push current. At the end, the heap contains the k largest.
CP Example: Merge K Sorted Arrays

Problem: Merge k sorted arrays into one sorted array. Use a min-heap storing (value, array_index, element_index). Pop the smallest, push the next element from the same array. This is O(n log k) where n is total elements — much better than O(nk) naive merge.
CP Example: Dijkstra's Algorithm Preview

Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm uses a priority queue to always expand the node with the smallest known distance. This greedy strategy guarantees the shortest path in graphs with non-negative weights. We'll cover this fully in the Graph Theory section.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of priority_queue::push()?
blocks.explanation: push() inserts an element and maintains the heap property by bubbling up, which takes O(log n) time where n is the current heap size.

blocks.question: How do you create a min-heap in C++?
blocks.explanation: The third template parameter is the comparator. greater<int> makes it a min-heap (smallest on top). The second parameter is the underlying container (must be a random-access container like vector).

blocks.question: Which priority_queue method returns the largest element without removing it?
blocks.explanation: top() returns a reference to the largest element (for max-heap) in O(1) time. pop() removes it but doesn't return the value — you must call top() first if you need it.

blocks.value: Binary Search — The O(log n) Powerhouse

Binary search is the most important algorithm in CP. It reduces search space by half each iteration, giving O(log n) time. But it's not just for finding elements — the **binary search on answer** technique solves optimization problems that seem to need brute force. Master this and you unlock 30% of CP problems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing binary search dividing sorted array in half repeatedly
blocks.caption: Binary search halves the search space each step — O(log n) vs O(n) linear

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A sorted array [1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15] with target 7. Show mid=9 (index 3), then left half [1,3,5,7], mid=3 (index 1), then right half [5,7], mid=5 (index 0), then [7]. Arrows showing the halving process. Label 'O(log n) steps'.
STL lower_bound and upper_bound

**lower_bound(first, last, x)** — returns iterator to first element >= x
**upper_bound(first, last, x)** — returns iterator to first element > x
**equal_range** — returns pair of both bounds

All are O(log n) on sorted ranges. They work on arrays, vectors, sets, and maps.

blocks.value: Manual Binary Search Implementation

Know how to write binary search manually. The key is avoiding infinite loops — use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` to prevent overflow, and carefully adjust lo and hi. There are two common patterns: finding exact match, and finding boundary conditions.
CP Example: Binary Search on Answer

Problem: Given n boards of lengths L[i], paint them with k painters where each painter paints contiguous boards. Minimize the maximum length painted by any painter. The answer lies between max(L[i]) and sum(L[i]). Binary search on the maximum length and check if k painters suffice.
CP Example: Aggressive Cows (Binary Search + Greedy)

Problem: Given n stalls and c cows, place cows in stalls such that the minimum distance between any two cows is maximized. Binary search on the minimum distance. For a given distance, greedily place cows and check if all c cows fit. This is a classic SPOJ/Codeforces problem.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of std::lower_bound on a sorted array?
blocks.explanation: lower_bound performs binary search on a sorted range, giving O(log n) time. It returns an iterator to the first element not less than the target.

blocks.question: In binary search on answer problems, what does the 'check' function typically do?
options: Verifies if a candidate answer is feasible
blocks.correctAnswer: Verifies if a candidate answer is feasible
blocks.explanation: In binary search on answer, you binary search over possible answers. The check function verifies if a given candidate answer can be achieved, allowing you to narrow the search space.

blocks.question: Which formula prevents integer overflow when calculating mid in binary search?
blocks.explanation: lo + (hi - lo) / 2 prevents overflow that could occur with (lo + hi) / 2 when lo and hi are large (e.g., near INT_MAX). This is a critical detail in CP.

blocks.value: Prefix Sum & Difference Array — Range Query Masters

**Prefix Sum** answers range sum queries in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing. **Difference Array** applies range updates in O(1) and computes the final array in O(n). Together, they solve a huge class of range query and range update problems that would otherwise need O(n) per query.

blocks.alt: Visual showing original array, prefix sum array, and how range sum is computed as pref[r] - pref[l-1]
blocks.caption: Prefix sum: pref[i] = sum of a[0..i]. Range sum [l,r] = pref[r] - pref[l-1].

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Three rows. Row 1: Original array a = [3,1,4,1,5]. Row 2: Prefix array pref = [3,4,8,9,14] with arrows showing cumulative sums. Row 3: Range sum [1,3] = pref[3] - pref[0] = 8 - 3 = 5, which equals a[1]+a[2]+a[3] = 1+4+1 = 6... wait, fix: [1,3] means indices 1 to 3: 1+4+1=6. pref[3]=8, pref[0]=3, 8-3=6. Show this calculation clearly.
Prefix Sum — 1D and 2D

1D: `pref[i] = pref[i-1] + a[i]`. Range sum [l,r] = `pref[r] - pref[l-1]`.
2D: `pref[i][j] = a[i][j] + pref[i-1][j] + pref[i][j-1] - pref[i-1][j-1]`. Submatrix sum uses inclusion-exclusion.
Difference Array — Range Updates

To add `val` to range [l,r]: `diff[l] += val`, `diff[r+1] -= val`. After all updates, compute prefix sum of diff to get the final array. This turns O(n) range updates into O(1) each — crucial for problems with many updates.
CP Example: Range Addition Queries
Problem: Given an array of zeros and q queries, each query adds v to range [l,r]. Print the final array. With difference array, each query is O(1) and final computation is O(n).
CP Example: Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's with Prefix)

Problem: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray. Kadane's algorithm is O(n), but the prefix sum approach (max subarray ending at i = pref[i] - min(pref[0..i-1])) gives the same result and is easier to extend to 2D.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of a range sum query with prefix sum?
blocks.explanation: After O(n) preprocessing to build the prefix array, each range sum query is O(1): sum[l,r] = pref[r+1] - pref[l]. This is the power of prefix sums.

blocks.question: In a difference array, how do you add 'val' to range [l,r]?
blocks.explanation: diff[l] += val starts the addition, diff[r+1] -= val cancels it after position r. When you compute the prefix sum of diff, the val applies exactly to indices [l,r].

blocks.question: Which technique allows O(1) range updates on an array?
blocks.explanation: The difference array technique allows O(1) range updates by marking start and end+1 positions, then computing the final array with a single prefix sum pass in O(n).

blocks.value: Two Pointers & Sliding Window — O(n) Magic

**Two Pointers** maintains two indices that move through the array in a coordinated way — often one from each end, or both from the start. **Sliding Window** maintains a subarray (window) that slides through the array, adjusting its bounds based on conditions. Both reduce O(n^2) brute force to O(n) by avoiding redundant work.

blocks.alt: Visual showing sliding window [left,right] moving across array, expanding and contracting
blocks.caption: Sliding window adjusts left and right pointers to maintain a valid subarray

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A horizontal array with a window [left, right] highlighted. Show three stages: 1) Window expands (right moves), 2) Window becomes invalid, 3) Window contracts (left moves) until valid again. Use arrows and color coding for the window boundary.
Two Pointers from Both Ends

Useful for: pair sum in sorted array, container with most water, trapping rain water, palindrome check. The key insight: if the array is sorted, you can eliminate half the search space with each comparison.
Sliding Window — Fixed Size

For problems requiring a fixed-size subarray: maintain a window of size k, compute the initial sum, then slide by subtracting the leftmost element and adding the new right element. This is O(n) vs O(nk) naive.
Sliding Window — Variable Size

For problems like 'longest substring with at most k distinct characters': expand the window by moving right, contract from left when the condition is violated. Track window state with a hash map or frequency array.
CP Example: Minimum Window Substring

Problem: Given strings s and t, find the minimum window in s that contains all characters of t. This is a hard sliding window problem (LeetCode 76). Use two frequency maps: one for t's requirements, one for the current window. Expand right until valid, then contract left to find minimum.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of the two-pointer technique on a sorted array?
blocks.explanation: Two pointers traverse the array at most once each. Even though there are two pointers, each element is visited at most once, giving O(n) total time.

blocks.question: In a variable-size sliding window, when do you move the left pointer?
options: When the window is too small
When the window violates the condition
blocks.correctAnswer: When the window violates the condition
blocks.explanation: The left pointer contracts the window when it becomes invalid (violates the problem condition). This maintains the invariant that the window is always valid between adjustments.

blocks.question: Which data structure is commonly used to track window contents in sliding window problems?
blocks.explanation: A hash map (or frequency array) tracks character/element frequencies in the current window, allowing O(1) checks for whether the window satisfies the problem conditions.

blocks.value: Bit Manipulation — The Low-Level Power Tool

Bit manipulation operates directly on the binary representation of integers. It's incredibly fast (single CPU instructions) and unlocks elegant solutions to problems involving subsets, parity, powers of two, and state compression. In CP, bitwise operations are often the difference between TLE and AC.

blocks.alt: Visual showing AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and shift operations on 8-bit numbers
blocks.caption: Bitwise operations work on every bit simultaneously — O(1) at the hardware level

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Two 8-bit numbers side by side (e.g., 01011010 and 00110111). Show four rows below: AND result, OR result, XOR result, NOT of first. Use color coding: green for 1s, gray for 0s. Label each operation clearly.
Essential Bitwise Operators

**& (AND)** — bit is 1 only if both bits are 1. Used for masking.
**|** (OR)** — bit is 1 if either bit is 1. Used for setting bits.
**^ (XOR)** — bit is 1 if bits differ. Used for toggling and finding unique elements.
**~ (NOT)** — flips all bits. Use with caution due to sign extension.
**<< (left shift)** — multiplies by 2^k. **>> (right shift)** — divides by 2^k.

All are O(1) and work on integers up to 64 bits (use `long long` for 64-bit masks).

Problem: Every element appears twice except one. Find the unique element. XOR of a number with itself is 0, and XOR with 0 is the number itself. XORing all elements cancels out pairs, leaving the unique element.
CP Example: Subset Sum with Bitset

blocks.explanation: Powers of 2 have exactly one bit set. n & (n-1) clears the rightmost set bit. If the result is 0, there was only one bit set, meaning n is a power of 2.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of iterating all subsets of n elements using bitmasks?
blocks.explanation: There are 2^n subsets. For each subset, checking all n bits to build the subset gives O(n) per subset, totaling O(2^n * n). With bit tricks, you can optimize to O(2^n) by only iterating set bits.

blocks.question: Which operator toggles a bit (0→1, 1→0) at position k?

blocks.value: Number Theory — The Foundation of CP Math

Number theory problems appear in almost every contest. GCD, LCM, prime factorization, and primality testing are building blocks for harder problems. The Euclidean algorithm for GCD is one of the oldest and most elegant algorithms in mathematics — and it's O(log min(a,b)).

The Euclidean algorithm is based on the principle that GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b). The remainder decreases rapidly, guaranteeing termination in O(log min(a, b)) steps. In C++17, use `std::gcd` and `std::lcm` from `<numeric>`. For older standards, `__gcd(a, b)` works in GCC.

A prime number is only divisible by 1 and itself. Naive primality test checks up to √n. For multiple queries, the **Sieve of Eratosthenes** precomputes primes up to n in O(n log log n). For very large n (up to 10^12), use **Miller-Rabin** deterministic test with specific bases.

Every integer can be uniquely expressed as a product of primes. Trial division up to √n works for n ≤ 10^9. For multiple queries with n ≤ 10^6, precompute smallest prime factors (SPF) using sieve for O(log n) factorization per query.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of the Euclidean GCD algorithm?
blocks.explanation: The Euclidean algorithm reduces the problem size by at least half every two steps (worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers). Thus it runs in O(log min(a,b)) time.

blocks.question: Why do we compute LCM as (a / gcd(a,b)) * b instead of (a * b) / gcd(a,b)?
options: It gives a more accurate result
It's required by the C++ standard
blocks.explanation: a * b can overflow 64-bit integers even when the LCM fits. Dividing first by GCD keeps the intermediate result smaller and prevents overflow.

blocks.question: What is the C++17 header for std::gcd and std::lcm?

blocks.value: Modular Arithmetic — Keeping Numbers Small

In CP, answers often need to be printed modulo 10^9+7 (a prime) or 10^9+9. Direct computation of factorials, powers, or combinations overflows even 64-bit integers. Modular arithmetic wraps numbers around, keeping them manageable while preserving mathematical structure.

blocks.alt: Visual showing modular arithmetic as a clock face wrapping around at modulus
blocks.caption: Modular arithmetic wraps around like a clock — numbers stay within [0, mod-1]

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A circular clock face labeled 0 to mod-1. Show an arrow from a large number wrapping around to its modulo position. Label key properties: (a+b)%m, (a*b)%m, and the concept of modular inverse.
Modular Operations & Properties

**(a + b) % m = ((a % m) + (b % m)) % m**
**(a - b) % m = ((a % m) - (b % m) + m) % m**  (add m to handle negatives)
**(a * b) % m = ((a % m) * (b % m)) % m**

**Division** requires modular inverse: (a / b) % m = (a * b^-1) % m. The inverse exists only if gcd(b, m) = 1. For prime m, b^-1 = b^(m-2) % m (Fermat's Little Theorem).

blocks.question: What is the modular inverse of a under prime modulus p?
blocks.explanation: By Fermat's Little Theorem, a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p and a not divisible by p. Thus a^(p-2) ≡ a^(-1) (mod p), which is the modular inverse.

blocks.question: Which theorem gives a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p?
blocks.explanation: Fermat's Little Theorem states that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). This is the foundation for computing modular inverses with fast exponentiation.

blocks.value: Combinatorics — Counting with Style

Combinatorics problems ask "how many ways?" — arrangements, selections, distributions, and paths. The answers grow exponentially, so modular arithmetic is essential. Master nCr, Catalan numbers, inclusion-exclusion, and the stars and bars method to tackle these problems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing Pascal's triangle with binomial coefficients highlighted
blocks.caption: Pascal's triangle gives binomial coefficients — each cell is sum of two above

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Pascal's triangle with rows 0 to 6. Highlight the path showing C(5,2) = 10. Show the recurrence C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k). Use warm colors for the triangle.
Binomial Coefficients — nCr

C(n, r) = n! / (r! * (n-r)!). For small n (≤ 1000), precompute using Pascal's identity: C(n,r) = C(n-1,r-1) + C(n-1,r). For large n with mod, precompute factorials and inverse factorials. For single queries with large n, use multiplicative formula with modular inverse.
Catalan Numbers

Catalan numbers appear in counting valid parentheses, binary trees, triangulations, and Dyck paths. C(n) = (1/(n+1)) * C(2n, n). The first few are 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429... Precompute using recurrence: C(n+1) = C(n) * 2*(2n+1) / (n+2).
Stars and Bars

Problem: Distribute n identical items into k distinct bins. The formula is C(n+k-1, k-1). If each bin must have at least 1 item, it's C(n-1, k-1). This solves many distribution and equation-solving problems.

blocks.explanation: Catalan numbers count valid parentheses sequences, binary trees, Dyck paths, and triangulations. C(n) = (1/(n+1)) * C(2n, n).

blocks.value: Sieve of Eratosthenes — Prime Generation at Scale

The Sieve of Eratosthenes is the most efficient way to find all primes up to n. It marks multiples of each prime starting from its square. Time complexity is O(n log log n) — essentially linear for practical purposes. For n up to 10^7, it runs in under a second.

blocks.alt: Visual showing sieve process: crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7 on a number grid
blocks.caption: Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross out multiples of each prime starting from p²

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A grid of numbers 1 to 50. Show progressive elimination: first cross out multiples of 2 (except 2), then multiples of 3 (except 3), then 5, then 7. Remaining unmarked numbers are primes. Use animation-style frames or color coding (red for eliminated, green for primes).
Classic Sieve Implementation

Use a boolean array `is_prime[]`. Start from 2, mark all multiples as non-prime. Optimization: start marking from i*i (smaller multiples already marked). Use `vector<char>` instead of `vector<bool>` for speed — `vector<bool>` is bit-packed and slower.

blocks.value: Sieve Optimizations

1. **Sieve till root**: Only iterate i up to √n. Inner loop starts at i*i.
2. **Skip evens**: Only sieve odd numbers after handling 2 separately. Cuts memory and time in half.
3. **Bitset**: Use `bitset<MAXN>` for compact memory, but `vector<char>` is often faster due to cache.
4. **Linear sieve**: Each composite is marked exactly once by its smallest prime factor. O(n) time.
Segmented Sieve — Large Range Primes

When n is too large for a full sieve (e.g., n = 10^12), use segmented sieve. Generate primes up to √n with classic sieve, then use them to mark composites in segments of size S (typically 10^4 to 10^5). Memory is O(√n + S) instead of O(n).
CP Example: Count Primes in Range [L,R]

Problem: Given multiple queries [L,R], count primes in each range. Precompute prefix sum array from sieve for O(1) queries. For large L,R, use segmented sieve per query or precompute with block decomposition.
Sieve Applications

Beyond prime generation, the sieve enables:
• **Smallest Prime Factor (SPF)** array for O(log n) factorization
• **Euler's Totient** φ(n) for all n up to limit
• **Mobius function** μ(n) for inclusion-exclusion
• **Number of divisors** and **sum of divisors** for all n
• **Prime counting function** π(n) via prefix sums

blocks.explanation: In the sieve, we start marking multiples from i*i because all smaller multiples of i (like i*2, i*3, ..., i*(i-1)) have already been marked by smaller primes. This is a crucial optimization.

blocks.value: Graph Theory — The Heart of CP

Graph problems dominate competitive programming contests. From social networks to road maps, from dependency resolution to game states — graphs model relationships between objects. Mastering graph algorithms is non-negotiable for any serious CP competitor. This part covers graph representation and Breadth-First Search (BFS), the foundation of all graph traversal.

blocks.alt: Visual comparison of adjacency list vs adjacency matrix for a sample graph
blocks.caption: Adjacency list is space-efficient for sparse graphs; matrix is fast for dense graphs

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Left: Adjacency list showing an array of linked lists. Node 0 → [1, 2], Node 1 → [0, 2, 3], etc. Right: Adjacency matrix as a 2D grid with 1s and 0s. Label space complexity: List O(V+E), Matrix O(V²). Highlight that CP almost always uses adjacency list.
Graph Representation in C++

**Adjacency List** (recommended for CP): `vector<vector<int>> adj(n)`. For weighted graphs: `vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> adj(n)` where pair is {neighbor, weight}. Space: O(V + E).

**Adjacency Matrix**: `vector<vector<int>> adj(n, vector<int>(n, 0))`. Space: O(V²). Only use when V ≤ 1000 or dense graph.

**Edge List**: `vector<tuple<int,int,int>> edges` for {u, v, w}. Used in Kruskal's and Bellman-Ford.
BFS — Breadth-First Search

BFS explores a graph level by level, starting from a source node. It uses a queue and guarantees the shortest path in **unweighted** graphs. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V).

**Key applications:**
• Shortest path in unweighted graphs
• Level-order traversal
• Connected components
• Bipartite graph checking
• 0-1 BFS (deque variant for 0/1 weighted edges)
BFS on Grid (2D)

Grid problems are extremely common in CP. Each cell is a node, edges connect to 4 (or 8) neighbors. BFS on grid finds shortest path in unweighted mazes. Use direction arrays `dx[] = {-1, 1, 0, 0}` and `dy[] = {0, 0, -1, 1}` for cleaner code.
CP Example: Connected Components (BFS)
Problem: Count connected components in an undirected graph. Run BFS from each unvisited node — each BFS discovers one component. This is a Codeforces Div 2 B/C staple.
CP Example: Bipartite Graph Check (BFS)

Problem: Check if a graph is bipartite (can be 2-colored such that no adjacent nodes have same color). BFS with coloring: assign color 0 to source, color 1 to neighbors, and check for conflicts. A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd-length cycles.

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
blocks.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued/dequeued once (O(V)) and each edge is examined once (O(E)). Total: O(V + E). This is optimal for graph traversal.

blocks.question: Which data structure is used in BFS?
blocks.explanation: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to process nodes level by level. Stack is used in DFS. Priority queue is used in Dijkstra's and A*.

blocks.question: What vector type represents a weighted adjacency list in C++?
blocks.explanation: vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> adj(n) stores for each node a list of {neighbor, weight} pairs. The outer vector has size n (nodes), inner vectors store edges.

parts.partTitle: Part 22: DFS, Cycle Detection & Topological Sort

blocks.value: DFS — Depth-First Search

DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. It uses a stack (explicit or recursion) and is the go-to algorithm for: detecting cycles, finding connected components, topological sorting, and solving many backtracking problems. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) for recursion stack.

blocks.alt: Visual showing DFS traversal tree with discovery and finish times marked on nodes
blocks.caption: DFS creates a depth-first tree — back edges indicate cycles in directed graphs

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A directed graph with nodes 0-5. Show DFS starting from 0, going deep: 0→1→2→3, then backtrack to 2, then 2→4, backtrack, etc. Mark discovery times (d) and finish times (f) on each node. Highlight tree edges (black), back edges (red — indicate cycle). Use a clean tree layout.
DFS Implementation — Recursive & Iterative

Recursive DFS is concise but risks stack overflow on deep graphs (>10^5 depth). Iterative DFS with an explicit stack avoids this. Track three states: 0=unvisited (white), 1=visiting (gray), 2=visited (black). Gray nodes with gray neighbors indicate a cycle in directed graphs.
Cycle Detection in Directed Graphs

A directed graph has a cycle iff DFS encounters a back edge (an edge from a gray node to another gray node). For undirected graphs, a cycle exists if we visit a node that's already visited and is NOT the parent.
Topological Sort — Kahn's Algorithm (BFS)

Topological sort orders nodes such that for every directed edge u→v, u comes before v. Only possible for DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs). Kahn's algorithm uses in-degree counting and a queue. Time: O(V + E).
Topological Sort — DFS-Based

DFS-based topological sort: run DFS, and after exploring all children, push the node onto a stack. Reverse the stack for the topological order. This naturally detects cycles (if a back edge is found during DFS).
CP Example: Course Schedule (Topological Sort)

Problem: There are n courses, some are prerequisites for others. Determine if you can finish all courses. This is exactly checking if the prerequisite graph is a DAG. If a cycle exists, it's impossible.
CP Example: Longest Path in DAG

Problem: Find the longest path in a Directed Acyclic Graph. This is NP-hard for general graphs but solvable in O(V+E) for DAGs using topological sort + DP. Process nodes in topological order and relax edges.

blocks.question: What data structure is used in iterative DFS?
blocks.explanation: DFS uses a stack (LIFO) to explore as deep as possible before backtracking. The recursive implementation implicitly uses the call stack.

blocks.question: When does a directed graph have a valid topological sort?
options: Only if it's a DAG (no cycles)
blocks.correctAnswer: Only if it's a DAG (no cycles)
blocks.explanation: Topological sort is only possible for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). If a cycle exists, there's no way to order nodes such that all edges go forward.

blocks.question: What are the three DFS node states used for cycle detection?
blocks.explanation: State 0 (white/unvisited), 1 (gray/visiting), 2 (black/visited). Finding an edge to a gray node indicates a back edge and thus a cycle in directed graphs.

blocks.value: Shortest Paths & Minimum Spanning Tree

This part covers the most important weighted graph algorithms: Dijkstra's (single-source shortest path), Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs shortest path), and Minimum Spanning Tree algorithms (Kruskal's and Prim's). These appear in almost every contest and are essential for solving optimization problems on weighted graphs.

blocks.alt: Visual comparison of Dijkstra's (greedy, one source), Floyd-Warshall (DP, all pairs), and MST (connect all nodes minimally)
blocks.caption: Dijkstra: single-source shortest path. Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest path. MST: minimal connection of all nodes.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Three panels. Left: Dijkstra's showing source node 0 with distance labels spreading outward. Middle: Floyd-Warshall showing a distance matrix being updated. Right: MST showing a tree connecting all nodes with minimal total edge weight. Label time complexities: Dijkstra O(E log V), Floyd O(V³), MST O(E log V).
Dijkstra's Algorithm — Single-Source Shortest Path

Dijkstra finds the shortest path from a source to all other nodes in a graph with **non-negative** edge weights. It uses a greedy approach: always expand the node with the smallest known distance. Implementation uses a priority queue (min-heap). Time: O(E log V) with binary heap.
Dijkstra with Set (Erase-Update Optimization)
Instead of pushing duplicate entries to the priority queue, use a set and erase the old entry when updating. This reduces memory and can be slightly faster, though the complexity remains O(E log V).
Floyd-Warshall — All-Pairs Shortest Path

Floyd-Warshall finds shortest paths between ALL pairs of nodes using dynamic programming. It works with negative edges (but not negative cycles). The DP state: `dist[i][j][k]` = shortest path from i to j using only nodes {0..k-1} as intermediates. Time: O(V³). Space: O(V²). Best for V ≤ 500.

blocks.value: Kruskal's MST — Union-Find

Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) connects all nodes with minimum total edge weight. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges by weight and greedily adds the smallest edge that doesn't form a cycle, using Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) for cycle detection. Time: O(E log E).
Prim's MST — Priority Queue

Prim's algorithm grows the MST from a starting node, always adding the cheapest edge connecting the tree to a non-tree node. Like Dijkstra but tracks minimum edge weight to the tree instead of distance from source. Time: O(E log V).
CP Example: Shortest Path with Exactly K Edges

Problem: Find the shortest path from source to target using exactly k edges. This is a classic DP on graphs problem. State: dp[i][v] = shortest path to v using exactly i edges. Transition: dp[i][v] = min(dp[i-1][u] + w(u,v)) for all edges into v. Time: O(k * E).

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap?
blocks.explanation: Each edge may cause a heap push (O(log V)), and there are E edges. Total: O(E log V). With a Fibonacci heap, this improves to O(V log V + E).

blocks.question: When should you use Floyd-Warshall over Dijkstra?
options: When you need all-pairs shortest paths and V ≤ 500
When edge weights are very large
When the graph has negative cycles
blocks.correctAnswer: When you need all-pairs shortest paths and V ≤ 500
blocks.explanation: Floyd-Warshall is O(V³) which is feasible only for V ≤ 500. For larger graphs or single-source queries, run Dijkstra from each source (O(V * E log V)) or use Johnson's algorithm.

blocks.question: What data structure does Kruskal's algorithm use for cycle detection?
blocks.explanation: Kruskal's uses the Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union / DSU) data structure to efficiently check if adding an edge would form a cycle. Without path compression and union by size, it would be too slow.

parts.partTitle: Part 24: Advanced Graph Algorithms — Bellman-Ford, SPFA & Johnson's

blocks.value: Handling Negative Weights & Advanced Shortest Paths

Dijkstra fails with negative edge weights because its greedy assumption — that the shortest path to a node is finalized once popped — breaks down. Bellman-Ford handles negatives by relaxing all edges repeatedly. SPFA is an optimized queue-based variant. Johnson's algorithm combines Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra for all-pairs shortest paths on sparse graphs with negative edges.

blocks.alt: Visual showing Dijkstra failing on negative edge vs Bellman-Ford correctly finding shorter path
blocks.caption: Negative edges can create shorter paths through already-visited nodes — Dijkstra misses these

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Two panels. Left: Dijkstra from A, edge A→B weight 5, A→C weight 2, C→B weight -4. Dijkstra picks B with dist 5 first, misses the A→C→B path of -2. Right: Bellman-Ford iterates all edges, finds the shorter path. Use red X on Dijkstra result, green check on Bellman-Ford.
Bellman-Ford Algorithm

Relax all edges (V-1) times. After V-1 iterations, all shortest paths (with at most V-1 edges) are found. Run one more iteration — if any distance improves, a negative cycle exists. Time: O(V * E). Works for directed graphs; for undirected, treat each edge as two directed edges.
SPFA — Shortest Path Faster Algorithm

SPFA is a queue-based optimization of Bellman-Ford. Instead of relaxing all edges blindly, it only relaxes edges from nodes whose distance was recently updated. Average case is much faster than O(VE), but worst case remains O(VE). Can be hacked on some platforms with adversarial graphs — use with caution in contests.
Johnson's Algorithm — All-Pairs with Negatives

Problem: All-pairs shortest path on a sparse graph with negative edges (but no negative cycles). Floyd-Warshall is O(V³). Johnson's runs Bellman-Ford once from a dummy source, then reweights all edges to be non-negative, then runs Dijkstra from every node. Total: O(V * E log V), much better for sparse graphs.

blocks.value: 0-1 BFS — Shortest Path with 0/1 Weights
Special case: all edge weights are 0 or 1. Use a deque instead of priority queue. Push to front for weight 0, push to back for weight 1. This gives O(V + E) time — faster than Dijkstra's O(E log V).
CP Example: Currency Exchange (Negative Cycle Detection)

Problem: Given exchange rates between currencies, detect if arbitrage is possible (a cycle where you end up with more money than you started). This is exactly detecting a negative cycle in a graph where edge weight = -log(exchange_rate).

blocks.question: What is the time complexity of Bellman-Ford?
blocks.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges (V-1) times, giving O(V * E). This is slower than Dijkstra but handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles.

blocks.question: When should you use 0-1 BFS instead of Dijkstra?
blocks.explanation: 0-1 BFS uses a deque and runs in O(V + E) for graphs with only 0/1 edge weights. It's asymptotically faster than Dijkstra's O(E log V) for this special case.

blocks.question: What does the extra iteration in Bellman-Ford detect?
blocks.explanation: After V-1 iterations, all shortest paths without cycles are found. If any distance can still be improved in the V-th iteration, a negative cycle exists that can be traversed infinitely to reduce distance.

blocks.value: Graph Structure — SCCs, Articulation Points & Bridges

Understanding the structural properties of graphs is crucial for solving many CP problems. Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) partition a directed graph into maximal subgraphs where every node is reachable from every other. Articulation points and bridges identify critical nodes and edges whose removal disconnects the graph. These concepts appear in network reliability, game theory, and condensation problems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing a directed graph condensed into SCCs forming a DAG
blocks.caption: Condensation graph: each SCC becomes a single node, resulting in a DAG

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Top: A directed graph with 8 nodes and cycles. Highlight three SCCs with different colors: {0,1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6,7}. Bottom: The condensation DAG with 3 super-nodes and edges between them. Show that the condensed graph is always a DAG. Label with 'Kosaraju's Algorithm' or 'Tarjan's Algorithm'.
Kosaraju's Algorithm — SCC in O(V + E)

Kosaraju's algorithm finds SCCs in two DFS passes: (1) DFS on original graph, pushing nodes to a stack in order of completion. (2) DFS on the transposed graph (all edges reversed), popping from the stack. Each DFS tree in the second pass is one SCC. Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V + E) for the transpose.
Tarjan's Algorithm — SCC in One Pass

Tarjan's algorithm finds SCCs using a single DFS with discovery times and low-link values. low[u] = min(discovery time of u, low-link of descendants, discovery times of nodes in stack reachable by back edge). When low[u] == disc[u], u is the root of an SCC — pop the stack until u. More memory-efficient than Kosaraju's (no transpose needed).

SCC 2: 4 3

blocks.value: Articulation Points & Bridges (Tarjan)

An articulation point (cut vertex) is a node whose removal increases the number of connected components. A bridge (cut edge) is an edge with the same property. Both are found using DFS with low-link values similar to SCC Tarjan's. For articulation points: root is AP if it has 2+ children; non-root u is AP if low[v] >= disc[u] for some child v. For bridges: edge (u,v) is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u].
CP Example: 2-SAT using SCC

2-SAT (2-satisfiability) is a classic problem: given boolean variables and clauses of form (a OR b), determine if there's a satisfying assignment. Each variable x has two nodes: x (true) and ¬x (false). Each clause (a OR b) implies two implications: ¬a → b and ¬b → a. The formula is satisfiable iff no variable and its negation are in the same SCC.

blocks.value: CP Example: Critical Connections (Bridges)

Problem: Given a network of servers connected by bidirectional connections, find all critical connections (bridges) — connections whose removal disconnects the network. This is LeetCode 1192 and a common interview/contest problem. Direct application of bridge-finding Tarjan's algorithm.

blocks.question: What is the key invariant in Tarjan's SCC algorithm?
options: low[u] == disc[u] when u is the root of an SCC
disc[u] < disc[v] for all edges u→v
blocks.correctAnswer: low[u] == disc[u] when u is the root of an SCC
blocks.explanation: In Tarjan's algorithm, when low[u] == disc[u], node u is the root of an SCC. All nodes in the stack above u belong to the same SCC. This is the fundamental condition for SCC extraction.

blocks.question: When is an edge (u,v) a bridge in an undirected graph?
blocks.explanation: Edge (u,v) is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u], meaning v cannot reach back to u or any ancestor of u without using edge (u,v). If low[v] >= disc[u], then u is an articulation point (for non-root nodes).

blocks.question: What is the condensation of a directed graph's SCCs?
blocks.explanation: The condensation graph, where each SCC is contracted to a single node, is always a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). This is because if there were a cycle in the condensation, those SCCs would merge into a single larger SCC.

blocks.value: Dynamic Programming — Breaking Problems into Subproblems

Dynamic Programming (DP) is the most important technique in competitive programming after graph algorithms. It solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing the results (memoization). The two key properties: Optimal Substructure (optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems) and Overlapping Subproblems (same subproblems recur many times). Master DP and you unlock 40% of contest problems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing Fibonacci recursion tree vs DP memoization table eliminating redundant calls
blocks.caption: DP eliminates redundant computation by storing and reusing subproblem solutions

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Left: Fibonacci recursion tree showing massive redundancy (f(3) computed multiple times). Right: DP table showing bottom-up computation with each value computed exactly once. Use red highlighting for redundant calls on left, green checkmarks on right. Label time: naive O(2^n) vs DP O(n).
Fibonacci — The Hello World of DP

Classic Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2). Naive recursion is O(2^n). Memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up) reduces to O(n). This illustrates the core DP transformation: recognize overlapping subproblems, store solutions, reuse.
Climbing Stairs — Count Ways

Problem: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count ways to reach step n. State: dp[i] = ways to reach step i. Transition: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] (come from 1 step below or 2 steps below). Base: dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1. This is Fibonacci in disguise — a common DP pattern.

blocks.output:
Input: 5
Ways to climb 5 stairs: 8
Ways with 1/2/3 steps: 13

blocks.value: House Robber — Decision DP

Problem: Rob houses in a line without robbing adjacent houses. Maximize loot. State: dp[i] = max loot from first i houses. Decision at each house: rob it (can't rob i-1, add dp[i-2] + a[i]) or skip it (dp[i-1]). Transition: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i]). This is the classic 'take or skip' DP pattern.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's DP)

Problem: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray. State: dp[i] = max subarray sum ending at index i. Transition: dp[i] = max(a[i], dp[i-1] + a[i]) — start fresh at i or extend previous subarray. Answer is max(dp[i]) over all i. This is the famous Kadane's algorithm, reducible to O(1) space.

blocks.value: DP on Grids — Minimum Path Sum

Problem: Given a grid with values, find the minimum sum path from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down. State: dp[i][j] = min sum to reach cell (i,j). Transition: dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base: dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]. This pattern extends to many grid DP problems.
The DP Framework — How to Approach Any DP Problem

**Step 1: Define the state.** What information do we need at each step? Usually dp[i] or dp[i][j] or dp[mask].

**Step 2: Formulate transitions.** How do we reach state (i,j) from previous states? Write the recurrence.

**Step 3: Identify base cases.** What are the smallest subproblems we can solve directly?

**Step 4: Determine the answer.** Which state(s) contain our final answer?

**Step 5: Optimize.** Can we reduce dimensions? Use rolling arrays? Space optimization?

Common DP patterns: Linear (1D array), Grid (2D array), Interval (dp[l][r]), Knapsack (dp[capacity]), Bitmask (dp[mask]), Tree (dp[node][state]), Digit (dp[pos][tight][sum]).

blocks.question: What are the two key properties a problem must have for DP to apply?
options: Sorted input and binary search applicability
blocks.explanation: Optimal substructure means the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblems are solved multiple times in a naive approach. Both are required for DP to be effective.

blocks.question: What is the space complexity of space-optimized Fibonacci?
blocks.explanation: Space-optimized Fibonacci only stores the last two values (a = F(i-2), b = F(i-1)), using O(1) extra space. This rolling variable technique is applicable to many 1D DP problems.

blocks.question: What technique stores computed subproblem results to avoid recomputation?
blocks.explanation: Memoization (top-down DP) stores results of expensive function calls and returns the cached result when the same inputs occur again. Tabulation (bottom-up) fills a table iteratively. Both avoid redundant computation.
